# Flexible Intelligent Metasurfaces for High-Mobility ISAC: Hardware Evidence, Adaptation Timescales, and Validation Gaps

---

## Abstract

A flexible intelligent metasurface (FIM) treats the physical shape of an aperture as a control variable alongside its electromagnetic state. Some recent system studies place that variable inside high-mobility integrated sensing and communication, where the delay–Doppler channel varies rapidly, and argue that shape adaptation follows it. This review asks whether existing hardware supports that argument: which operations in a FIM-assisted high-mobility link plausibly require fast adaptation, which may run on slower geometric or statistical timescales, and what has been measured about either?

We separate the architecture classes the FIM evidence base draws on, decompose FIM adaptation into ten stages from sensing to stabilised radiation, and record every timing value with its timed object, start and end events, and measurement status. No reviewed platform measures the duration of more than four of the ten stages, and the platform that reaches four has no radio-frequency layer. The two best-covered platforms do not overlap where it matters: one commands its shape but does not radiate, and the other radiates but cannot command its shape. No independently measured settling or post-deformation calibration duration is reported in the reviewed set, and stabilised radiation is timed only with geometry held static. Tracing the hardware-feasibility premises of the FIM system literature back to their primary sources shows element-level response times presented as surface morphing periods, and a tabulated value with no counterpart in the cited source.

The contribution is the audit and the reporting discipline it motivates; we propose no hardware and do not claim the architecture is infeasible.

**Index terms** — Flexible intelligent metasurface, reconfigurable intelligent surface, integrated sensing and communication, high mobility, adaptation latency, hardware validation, evidence synthesis, conformal metasurface.

---

## 1. Introduction

A reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) changes how it scatters by changing the electromagnetic state of its meta-atoms. A flexible intelligent metasurface (FIM) changes how it scatters by changing where its elements are. In the system-level formulation, each radiating element carries a coordinate along the surface normal, and the vector of those coordinates defines the surface shape. That shape enters the array response through the propagation phase, and is then optimised jointly with beamforming or sensing objectives, subject to a morphing range [1, Eqs. (1a)–(3), p. 13321; 2, Eq. (1)]. Simulated gains are reported across several formulations: a transmit-power reduction of about 3 dB at a one-wavelength morphing range for a multiuser downlink [2], further gains from introducing and then optimising a surface in a doubly dispersive multiple-input multiple-output ISAC setting [1, p. 13328], and element movement reported as more effective than passive phase control at enhancing received signal strength in a single-input single-output multipath scenario, with joint optimisation better still [3, p. 6823].

Geometry control differs from electronic state control in one respect that matters here: exercising it requires moving matter. An electromagnetic state change propagates at the speed of the tuning mechanism, whereas a geometry change is limited by actuator dynamics, structural response and damping. The system models do not represent that difference, and they need not: in all four FIM system papers reviewed here the shape is simply a variable that may be set, and the mechanism that sets it lies outside the model.

In quasi-static conditions, idealising the actuation may matter little for system-level performance. Under high mobility the timing assumptions may carry real weight, because the state the surface was configured for goes on changing while the surface responds. At the operating point of the high-mobility FIM–ISAC study reviewed here, 28 GHz and a maximum velocity of 208 m/s, the maximum Doppler shift is approximately 19.4 kHz.¹ A millimetre-wave carrier combined with a velocity of that order places the system outside the conditions under which the reviewed flexible and reconfigurable-surface hardware has been characterised. Those demonstrations span a wide range of carriers, but none is characterised under mobility of this kind.

Doppler frequency, coherence interval and the update deadline set by a specific system requirement are three different quantities, and they should not be treated as interchangeable. Doppler frequency follows from carrier and velocity, so 19.4 kHz is exact given the stated parameters. A coherence interval, by contrast, is a threshold-dependent correlation statistic, and the threshold is a choice whose consequences are measurable. In a RIS-assisted high-mobility study at 2.6 GHz with a user moving at 90 mph, the interval over which the time-correlation function exceeds 0.5 covers 51 symbols; the same paper's bit-error-rate comparison uses 20 symbol periods at 0.95 correlation and 40 at 0.82 [4, p. 721 and Fig. 4(b), p. 728]. One scenario therefore yields three answers spanning a factor of 2.5. An update deadline requires something further, a performance tolerance that somebody has selected, and this review defines none. The Doppler figure on its own establishes a regime, strongly time-selective, but not an interval. Without a deadline, asking whether the surface is fast enough has no answer, and the question this review can address is which operations in the loop are bound to the fast-varying state at all.

The obvious next question is how quickly a flexible metasurface reconfigures. The reviewed literature reports several such intervals, but they do not describe the same quantity. A scalable one-bit PIN-diode RIS reports an update time below 0.1 ms in its abstract and a tile reconfiguration below 10 ms in its results section [5]; both are correct, both bound the same 16 × 16 tile, and neither ends at a stated electromagnetic criterion, so the two orders of magnitude between them record a change of context, not a change of speed. On a liquid-crystal RIS the figures are approximately 15 ms and 72 ms, the switch-on and switch-off transitions of a 4.6 μm material layer between 10 % and 90 % thresholds [6]. A flexible microwave metasurface reports 16.76 ms for an interval running from shape acquisition to bias-voltage supply, which contains neither the deformation that produced the shape nor any settling afterwards [7]. For a soft shape-programmable surface the values are approximately 30 ms for an isolated ribbon and approximately 300 ms for a full surface developing from flat [8]. These four numbers are not competing estimates of one quantity. They measure different quantities, on different architectures, with different definitions of when the clock starts and stops, so quoting any one of them as *the* FIM response time yields a figure with no defined referent. Separating them is the task this review undertakes.

Three broad reviews in the reviewed set border this territory, and between them they leave a specific hole. Saifullah *et al.* classify tunable metasurfaces by tuning mechanism and rank their speeds qualitatively, with electrical tuning preferred above kilohertz modulation rates, liquid crystal below about 1 kHz, microfluidic tuning on a millisecond scale, and mechanically stretchable substrates slow, environmentally sensitive and unable to address individual unit cells; ISAC is not discussed [9]. Tishchenko *et al.* survey multi-functional and hybrid RIS for ISAC, treat controller and network latency as a practical constraint, and link higher carrier frequencies to shorter coherence times, with no discussion of mechanical tuning [10]. Closest to our own position is the survey of reconfigurable and movable antennas by Ma *et al.*: mechanical movement is generally slower than electronic reconfiguration; instantaneous-CSI position optimisation suits quasi-static environments with long coherence times, while fast fading calls for statistical-CSI approaches that reduce movement frequency; and hierarchical cross-layer control, in which statistical information guides slow movement while rapid state changes are decoupled, is an open direction [11, §I-C, §III-B4, §V-A]. The same survey argues that future models should incorporate inertia, settling time, friction, backlash, movement accuracy and energy rather than idealised instantaneous positioning [11, §V-C].

That prior work constrains what the present manuscript may claim. The slow-geometry, fast-electronics division of labour is established prior art, not a novelty available to this review or to any FIM paper: statistical-CSI FIM optimisation has been published [12, 13], a two-rate schedule of element movement per subframe and phase adjustment per time slot is already embedded in a FIM channel-estimation protocol [3, p. 6829], and delay-aware modelling of reconfigurable apertures has begun in the adjacent fluid-antenna literature [14]. None of the three reviews, however, treats FIMs as a dedicated architecture under those terms: a full-text search of each returns no occurrence of "FIM" or "flexible intelligent metasurface", which establishes the absence of explicit treatment under that label rather than the absence of conceptually related coverage.² Ma *et al.* recommend that models include movement time, settling and energy; no reviewed source establishes which of those quantities have been measured, on what object, or under what definition.

A FIM-dedicated overview article does exist outside the reviewed set, and the external search recorded in Section 2 did not return it. It introduces FIM hardware architectures, sets out application scenarios and case studies, and states this review's question in almost these terms: whether the surface "can morph fast enough to track small-scale fading remains uncertain", and "if morphing speed is slower than the channel coherence time, instantaneous channel-aware designs may become impractical" [15, p. 10]. An independent group arriving at the same uncertainty is corroboration, not pre-emption, and we treat it as such. What that article does not do is what the four contributions below do. It decomposes no adaptation chain into stages; it records no value with a timed object, a start event and an end event — it reports no numeric timing value at all, and its hardware table classifies shape reconfiguration qualitatively; and it traces none of the hardware-feasibility premises of the FIM system literature back to the primary measurements those premises rest on. Those are the gaps this review addresses, and they are unaffected by its existence.

The question examined here is therefore:

> Which operations in a FIM-assisted high-mobility ISAC system must track fast channel variation, which may follow slower geometric or statistical change, and how well are the resulting timescales supported by existing hardware and control demonstrations?

We answer it as an evidence-mapping problem, not a design problem. Within the literature reviewed here and the searches recorded in Section 2, the contributions are four.

**C1 — Architecture-aware adaptation-chain framework.** FIM adaptation is decomposed into ten stages from sensing to stabilised radiation, and each source's treatment of each stage is coded on two axes: what the source establishes about the stage, and what it establishes about how long the stage takes. Applied to the reviewed set, no platform measures the duration of more than four of the ten stages, and the platform reaching four has no radio-frequency layer.

**C2 — Definition-preserving timing register.** Every reported value is recorded with its timed object, start event, end event and measurement status, and values may be compared only within a comparability class. Two common simplifications fail that test: an element-level update time cannot stand in for an aperture-level configuration time, as one panel's own two bounds show; and the reported ranges for electronic and mechanical processes overlap once the tuning mechanism is named, so an architecture label alone does not order them.

**C3 — Traceability audit of the hardware-feasibility premises.** Three premises from the FIM system literature are traced to the primary measurements behind them. Among the 13 of 20 candidate citing studies whose full texts were accessible, four reuse a timing value with its scope changed, and those four form one connected co-authorship network; the remainder cite the same hardware and attach no timing value at all. Every count is a lower bound on a partially observed set, and no prevalence claim is made. Section 5.2 gives the instances and the bounds.

**C4 — Validation gap and reporting set.** Four intervals are unmeasured in the reviewed set, and the reporting fields we propose prescribe definitions — object, start event, end event — rather than acceptance thresholds.

We propose no hardware, no algorithm and no control architecture. The manuscript is an audit, and it rests on the accuracy of its citations.

## 2. Review scope and method

This is a structured critical review. It is not a systematic review, a systematic mapping study or a scoping review, and it does not adopt PRISMA terminology, because it does not satisfy the requirement those labels carry: a reproducible, protocol-driven, multi-database *search*. It does have a reproducible *extraction* protocol, and search and extraction are treated as separate things throughout.

**Corpus.** The reviewed set comprises 24 distinct research contributions across 34 files. They are *distinct* but not *independent*: several share authors, and duplicate versions, conference-and-journal pairs and same-group design lineages were collapsed into independence groups so that related publications are never counted as mutual confirmation of one another. Four of the files are supplementary-information or peer-review documents belonging to two of the papers; they are evidence *about* those papers, not evidence alongside them. Three sources were readable only as page images, and no load-bearing claim is drawn from them.

The corpus was assembled by convenience rather than by a protocol-driven database query, so inclusion criteria are stated retrospectively and describe what the set *is* instead of a prospective filter: peer-reviewed articles, preprints and author manuscripts concerning FIM system modelling; flexible or conformal reflective and transmissive metasurface hardware; programmable mechanical surface actuation; electronically reconfigurable RIS hardware reporting timing or power; high-mobility channel estimation for reconfigurable surfaces; and reviews of any of these. Sources with no wireless, electromagnetic or mechanical-actuation content were excluded.

One exclusion needs stating rather than leaving to the criteria, because it is where the strongest counterexample to this review's structural finding sits. A separate literature builds radiating apertures whose *shape* changes: origami and 4D-printed antennas and reflecting surfaces with shape-memory-polymer hinges, and mechanically reconfigured arrays more generally. It is adjacent to the FIM formulation rather than inside it, and the difference is in the control variable. The FIM system model audited here assigns each element a coordinate along the surface normal and optimises the vector of those coordinates [1, Eqs. (1a)–(3), p. 13321]. These platforms instead change a fold angle, an in-plane spacing or a global curvature, through a thermal or mechanical mechanism that is not addressed per element and, in the cases we located, is not commanded by a controller at all. Two of them are nonetheless close enough to bear on the argument, and both are cited and confronted in Sections 3.1 and 5.3 rather than excluded silently [16, 17]. The boundary is a definitional one and we state it as such: a reader who draws it differently should read the empty cell of Figure 1 and gap G1 accordingly.

Six sources were first read as preprints or author manuscripts; publisher-deposited records confirm versions of record for all six, and the published full texts of the three carrying the most weight were obtained and inspected. Every load-bearing timing and parameter quantity keyed to them survives at the published locators, which this manuscript cites. One non-timing claim did not survive that check, and the affected statement is not used here (Supplementary Section S3). Version-of-record status was checked for each source and then checked again immediately before completion, since publisher deposits appear after a preprint has been read. That second check established or corrected the recorded status of five entries, and the versions it established are the ones cited here. For the survey among them, the published record and page range were verified, but the version-of-record full text was not available to us, so passage-specific page locators into that version could not be checked. Locators to it are therefore given as section numbers, and the passages behind them were verified in the held preprint.

**External searches.** Two searches supplement the corpus, and their evidential weight differs. A documented but non-systematic external search (ten queries, 17 August 2026) established whether a FIM-specific review exists, whether two-timescale or statistical-CSI FIM control is already published, whether any measured FIM actuation latency exists, and where the hardware-feasibility timing claims in the FIM system literature originate. It used a general web-search interface, which does not expose reproducible hit counts, so its results are recorded as search outcomes, not as established absences. One of those outcomes was a false negative. That search concluded that no FIM-specific overview existed, when one had already been publicly available as a preprint for five months; it was retrieved by the targeted searches described next, and it is cited in Section 1 [15]. Two further targeted searches were run on 3 September 2026 against reproducible programmatic interfaces (the arXiv, Crossref and Europe PMC APIs): one repeated the overview question, the other tested the corpus boundary against morphing, origami and 4D-printed radiating apertures. The second located the platform discussed in Sections 3.1 and 5.3 [16, 17]. Both searches are recorded with their services, terms, dates and inclusion rationale in the search log; neither is exhaustive, and neither is claimed to be.

A forward citation search (18 August 2026) is reproducible, though its two stages are reproducible in different senses. Stage one is automatic and deterministic for the dated search: every work citing the three primary hardware sources was retrieved through the OpenAlex citation graph, giving 306 records and 262 unique works after deduplication by identifier, of which 65 passed a title-and-abstract screen against an explicit wireless and communications expression. Stage two is manual and recorded rather than re-derived: excluding optics, photonics, materials, mechanics and imaging work, and collapsing versions under the independence rule below, leaves **20 distinct flexible-metasurface or reconfigurable-surface system studies**, of which 13 were read in full and 7 are behind publisher paywalls with no open deposit located. No access control was circumvented, and every count arising from this search is a lower bound. The seed identifiers, the query, the deduplication rule, the screening expression, the per-work decision table and the retrieved records as they stood on 18 August 2026 are available as runnable code and data in the accompanying public reproducibility repository.³ Re-running that code against the preserved records reproduces the retrieval and this screen exactly. A live re-query may return a different set, because OpenAlex is updated continuously. Supplementary Section S5 gives the full flow and the study-family register.

**Extraction.** Extraction, unlike search, followed a fixed protocol applied uniformly to every source. We assign each source to an architecture class under explicit transfer rules (Section 3), code its treatment of each of the ten adaptation stages (Section 3), and enter every reported timing value in a register carrying its timed object, a named start event, a named end event, a measured/simulated/projected/derived flag, the architecture on which it was obtained, and a comparability class. Two values may be compared only if their comparability classes intersect.

Four principles govern the coding. Each exists because a specific confusion is possible without it. The complete symbolic scheme, the seven-level evidence ladder used to grade evidence from analytical derivation through prototype measurement to end-to-end closed-loop validation, and the per-source coded matrix are in Supplementary Section S6.

1. *Stage evidence and stage duration are separate questions.* A measured radiation pattern is a quantitative result and not a timing; a fully delimited *simulated* runtime is a timing and not a measurement. Both are routine in this literature, and a single code would misread both.
2. *An accuracy is never timing evidence.* A root-mean-square deviation, a displacement error or any other accuracy figure remains an accuracy, however quantitative it is. We also distinguish a measured stage duration from duration information available only as a stated share, component or residual of a larger aggregate; from a rate; and from an interval the experimenter deliberately allocated. Only the first licenses the verb *times*.
3. *Evidence is never upgraded.* A system simulation is not hardware validation, a measured actuator is not a radiating system, an electronic switching time is not a mechanical settling time, and a protocol unit — a subframe, a time slot, an iteration count — is not a duration, since none of the sources reporting them supplies the numerology needed to convert.
4. *Independence is tested, not assumed.* A preprint and its version of record are two versions of one study; a conference paper and its journal extension are one lineage; supplementary material belongs to its parent paper; and independence between citing works is tested by author-set intersection rather than inferred from differing first authors.

**Absence claims.** Every statement about what is missing is reduced to one of two checkable forms: *this named document does not report quantity Q*, or *across the N sources in this named table, no row records Q*. No statement about the field as a whole is made anywhere in this manuscript. Absence of a measurement in the literature we read is not evidence that the measurement does not exist, still less that the capability is unattainable.

One further constraint runs through everything downstream. No reviewed source reports a repetition count or a dispersion figure for its headline response, morphing or adaptation interval, so none of the values on which this review's arguments turn carries an uncertainty. One subordinate process quantity does carry a dispersion, a function-evaluation cycle stated as 0.35 ± 0.15 s, so the deficiency is specific to the headline intervals and not universal. It is a deficiency in the sources, not in the extraction, and additional literature cannot retroactively supply uncertainty for values already published without it.

## 3. FIM architectures and adaptation timescales

### 3.1 Architecture classes, and what may transfer between them

Evidence about FIM feasibility is drawn from seven physically distinct kinds of system, and a statement true of one is routinely false of another. A response time measured on a filamentary mechanical mesh, an update rate measured on a rigid PIN-diode panel and a compensation loop measured on a bending varactor-loaded sheet do not describe one technology. They describe three, whose measurements are nonetheless quoted in support of a single architecture. Only A1 through A4 are named as flexible or morphing metasurfaces by the literature that uses them, and even there the naming is inconsistent; A5 to A7 appear because the FIM literature draws evidence from them, not because their authors claim the label. The transfer rules at the end of this subsection depend on keeping them apart.

Three questions distinguish the classes: what physically changes, whether the change is imposed from outside or commanded by the system, and whether the radio-frequency state is independently programmable. Table 1 answers them alongside the questions that decide what a measurement is worth.

**Table 1 — Architecture classes drawn on by the FIM evidence base.** A1–A4 are the direct classes; A5–A7 are comparator or evidence-donor classes whose authors do not generally use the FIM label.

| Class | What it is | What changes | Deformation source | RF state programmable | RF measured | Mobility evidence | Representative sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A1** | Theoretical FIM array with independently movable elements | element coordinates | an optimisation variable — no mechanism specified | in some formulations | ✗ — no hardware | simulated only | [1], [2], [3], [18] |
| **A2** | Flexible **passive** reflective metasurface | sheet curvature | external | ✗ | ✓ at fixed curvatures | ✗ | [19], [20] |
| **A3** | Externally deformed, shape-aware **programmable** reflective surface | curvature **and** meta-atom state | external | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | [7], [21] |
| **A4** | Actively self-morphing mechanical surface | commanded local displacement | **self-actuated** | **no RF layer at all** | ✗ | ✗ | [8], [22] |
| **A5** | Rigid electronically reconfigurable RIS | meta-atom state only | none | ✓ | ✓ | modelled / simulated only ([4]) | [4] (modelled), [5], [6] |
| **A6** | Movable / reconfigurable antenna system | position, orientation or internal state | self-actuated | ✓ (RA sub-class) | outside the reviewed measurement scope | — | [11] (review) |
| **A7** | Flexible **active** antenna array | sheet curvature | external | ✓ (per-element RFIC) | ✓ | ✗ | [23], [24] |

No source in the reviewed set demonstrates A1 hardware. The FIM system papers define the surface as a coordinate vector constrained to a morphing range and entering the array response through the propagation phase [1, Eqs. (1a)–(3), p. 13321]; they specify no actuator, no sheet mechanics, no inter-element mechanical coupling and no fabrication route. Where physical plausibility is argued, two mechanical platforms are cited: a liquid-metal microfluidic network in an elastomeric matrix, and an array of metallic filaments actuated by distributed Lorentz forces [1, p. 13320], citing [8] and [22] respectively. That is a plausibility argument and should be read as one. Both cited platforms are A4, and carry no meta-atoms, no bias network, no dielectric substrate and no radio-frequency ground plane. When a flexible reflective microwave surface was actually built, achieving mechanical flexibility required replacing a solid copper ground with a serpentine mesh, a change reported to reduce estimated bending stiffness by more than two orders of magnitude [7, p. 3].

The two realised surfaces in the reviewed set that are simultaneously flexible, reflective and electronically programmable are A3, and they share a property that the A1 formulation reverses. In the flexible microwave metasurface with shape-guided adaptive programming [7], a 480 × 240 mm sheet carrying 32 × 16 meta-atoms is bent by an external mechanical platform, a conformal array of 32 strain sensors reconstructs the resulting shape, and a trained neural network maps that shape to the column bias voltages that restore the intended electromagnetic behaviour. The conformal reconfigurable reflectarray built from polydimethylsiloxane and printed liquid metal [21] takes a different route: a 10 × 10 array at 9 GHz with per-element PIN diodes achieves ±45° beam scanning using element-level conformal compensation phase, mounted on acrylic supports of different bending degrees. Each curvature is therefore a separate static experiment, and the surface neither senses nor commands its shape. Geometry is a disturbance to be compensated in both cases. In the A1 formulation geometry is the *primary control variable* — the thing chosen to maximise an objective — and the channel is what is being tracked. Within the reviewed set, no source demonstrates that inversion in hardware.

The two A4 platforms supply every measured mechanical timescale in this review, and neither has an electromagnetic function. The filamentary mechanical metasurface [22] is a 4 × 4 mesh of thin metal and polyimide traces on an 18.0 mm sample, driven by distributed Lorentz forces, and uniquely in the reviewed set it closes a loop on shape, with in-situ stereo imaging feeding an experiment-driven inverse design. The soft shape-programmable surface [8] uses liquid-metal microfluidic ribbons in an elastomer, and can fix a programmed shape through a liquid-metal phase transition, a mechanism by which a slowly-set geometry could in principle be held without continuous actuation. These are the right platforms to cite for mechanical feasibility and the wrong platforms to cite for a FIM response time, a distinction Section 5 shows has not always been maintained.

Two adjacent bodies of work bound the problem from outside. A large conformal literature concerns apertures whose shape is known and does not change, and it establishes two different things that should not be run together. Validated *design methods* exist for important fixed-curvature cases: integral-equation synthesis accounting for finite size, coupling and spatial dispersion [25]; a reduced-order coupled-dipole model of a cylindrically conformal waveguide-fed metasurface [26]; and cylindrical RIS design carried from surface-impedance synthesis to a one-bit unit-cell design, evaluated in full-wave simulation and not fabricated, with prototype measurement stated by its authors as future work [27]. Separately, *measured hardware* exists across several bands and phase resolutions: an active conformal metasurface lens [28]; a 3D-printed curved two-bit coding surface [29]; and a flexible liquid-metal-on-PDMS reflectarray holding its radiation characteristics across a ±25 % bending range at a fixed coding pattern [20]. Design evidence and measurement evidence are different levels on the ladder of Supplementary Section S6, and this review does not let one stand in for the other. That is prior art, not closure, and it is prior art about a different problem: curvature is a design parameter there, not a control variable. Flexible active antenna arrays (A7) supply the strongest evidence that large flexible coherent apertures are realisable, with two 256-element, 30 × 30 cm arrays remaining fully functional and programmable at concave and convex bend radii below 23 cm under closed-loop focusing driven by feedback from a remote receiver, and calibration explicitly targeting phase offsets caused by manufacturing variation, shape deformation and environmental change [23].

Four transfer rules follow, and are applied without exception in the remainder of the manuscript. A4 timing does not transfer to A1 or A3 without qualification, because A4 platforms have no radio-frequency layer and their measured response times bound a different mechanical object. An A5 electronic switching time is not a mechanical settling time. An A3 partial-loop latency is not a full-loop latency. And A7 is not A5: an active array's calibration architecture, which senses through its own transmit chain and closes a loop against a remote beacon, does not carry over to a passive reflective aperture, which has neither.

Figure 1 shows what this implies for the evidence base. Its two axes are properties of an experiment — has the platform demonstrated commanded physical geometry, and has radio-frequency performance been measured on it — so only platforms that performed an experiment are plotted; a modelling paper answers neither question, and placing simulation work in a hardware quadrant would be a category error. Three of the four cells are populated: the commanded-geometry-without-measured-RF cell by the two A4 mechanical platforms [8, 22], and the measured-RF-without-commanded-geometry cell by every A2, A3, A5 and A7 platform in the reviewed set on which radio-frequency performance was actually measured [5, 6, 7, 19, 20, 21, 23, 28, 29, 30, 31]. The conformal cylindrical RIS [27] is cited in this subsection as design evidence and does not appear in the map, because it reports no experiment of either kind. The cell requiring commanded geometry *and* measured radio-frequency performance together is empty. A1 does not occupy a cell in that map. It identifies the empty one, because the A1 system model specifies an operating point — geometry chosen by the optimiser, on an aperture whose radiation is what the optimisation is for — and not physical evidence to be classified.

The empty cell is a statement about the reviewed set, and one platform outside that set comes close enough that leaving it unstated would misrepresent the field. A 4D-printed intelligent reflecting surface operating at 27.2 GHz carries 225 PIN diodes across fifteen printed substrate columns over a silver-paste ground, and those columns are mounted on a multimaterial structure whose shape-memory-polymer hinges change the gaps between them. Both degrees of freedom are exercised on the same aperture: the diode states steer the beam, the column spacing changes which angles are reachable, and the scattering patterns are measured at two spacings, yielding measured directions of −46°/+50°, −22°/+14° and −16°/+12° that the fixed-geometry configuration does not reach. The paper also reports a duration for the geometric change — 240 s to recover from a column spacing of 0 mm to 2 mm — and concludes from it that the prototype is difficult to deploy under dynamic conditions such as vehicle communications [16]. A closely related platform thermally morphs a 4D-printed Miura-origami array and reports its maximum beam direction changing from 0° to 50° at 2.4 GHz, with recovery to the memorised state [17]; we read that result in its abstract and did not obtain its full text, so nothing further is drawn from it and no timing is taken from it at all.

The implications do not all point the same way. A radiating aperture with a programmable electromagnetic layer and a geometry that changes has been built and measured, so the combination is not unrealised in the wider literature, and Section 5's first validation gap is stated against that fact rather than around it. The geometric variable, however, is not the one the FIM formulation controls. A1 assigns each element a coordinate along the surface normal and optimises the vector of those coordinates; this platform changes an in-plane column spacing, and it changes it by heating the structure to 65 °C, deforming it with an external force, and cooling it, the return being a shape-memory recovery to one memorised state. It has two geometries instead of a coordinate vector, and a controller selects neither of them. By the definitions of this section it is neither A1 hardware nor a commanded-geometry platform. We therefore treat it as an adjacent boundary case, confronted here in the text rather than plotted in the reviewed-set map of Figure 1. The 240 s figure, finally, is itself an instance of what Section 5 is about. It is reported without a named start event, a named end event or an electromagnetic criterion, so what it bounds is the recovery of a printed structure and not the onset of trustworthy radiation after that recovery. The reporting fields this review proposes would have made the difference visible on the page.

> **Figure 1.** *Architecture–evidence map of the reviewed hardware.* Both axes are properties of an experiment, so only platforms that performed one are plotted; the theoretical FIM performs none and is drawn as an annotation on the empty cell rather than as a platform. Within the reviewed set, commanded geometry and measured radio-frequency performance have not been demonstrated together. The bound matters: one platform outside the reviewed set does change a printed geometry and measure radiation on the same aperture, and the text above states what it supplies and what it does not. *(File: `figures/fig1_architecture_evidence_map.pdf`.)*

### 3.2 The adaptation chain

FIM adaptation names a sequence, not an event, and the sequence crosses three physical domains — perception, computation and mechanics — which have no reason to share a magnitude. Decomposing it makes it possible to say *which process a given number times*, and it turns an apparently contradictory set of reported latencies into a consistent one.

| Stage | | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Sensing / acquisition | physical observation of the surface or environment — strain sensors, imaging, received pilots |
| S2 | Geometry estimation | conversion of raw sensor data into a surface-shape estimate |
| S3 | Channel estimation | acquisition of instantaneous or statistical channel state |
| S4 | Optimisation / inference | computation of the desired geometry and phase configuration |
| S5 | Control transmission | transport of the command from the compute element to the surface controller |
| S6 | Electronic state update | meta-atom electromagnetic state change |
| S7 | Mechanical morphing | the commanded physical displacement |
| S8 | Mechanical settling | decay of transient motion to within tolerance of the target shape |
| S9 | Calibration | re-establishment of the geometry-to-RF-response mapping after the shape changed |
| S10 | Stabilised RF operation | the interval over which the configured surface delivers its intended behaviour |

S1 spans two observation tasks with different drivers, and the distinction matters once timescales are discussed. Geometry sensing, written S1-G, follows deformation of the aperture; channel or pilot acquisition, written S1-C, follows the channel state and is what feeds S3. These are analytical sublabels used only where a timescale requirement is at issue. They are not additional stages: S1 remains one stage of ten for every coverage count, duration count and coded cell in this review.

Across the four reviewed FIM system papers — three distinct studies, since one is a short version of another — stages S5 through S9 are absent from the model or assumed instantaneous. Geometry takes the value the optimiser assigns it, at the moment the optimiser assigns it. Section 4 records what has been measured for each stage, and Supplementary Section S6 gives the per-source coded matrix from which those counts are taken.

### 3.3 What the surface is being asked to track

Treating "the channel" as one clock obscures how many states a FIM-assisted ISAC system is actually tracking, at different rates and with different consequences for failure. They are instantaneous complex fading, driven by Doppler; channel statistics and spatial correlation, deliberately treated as slower; angles of arrival and departure, which follow the user's traverse across the cell rather than the fading; target kinematics in the sensing subproblem; blockage, which is event-like, not periodic; the geometry of the aperture itself; and the calibration state that determines when the aperture may be trusted again after a shape change. High-mobility models update angles explicitly and separately from fading correlation [4], and communication and sensing may impose different movement and update requirements [11, §IV-B]. The reviewed set fixes no relative rates among these states, and none of them carries an update deadline, because assigning one requires a performance tolerance the reviewed sources do not supply. Supplementary Table S7 records each state with its driver, the control variable it binds, and the evidence available for it.

Everything turns on which of these states drives the shape optimisation. That slow-geometry reading is not this review's reconstruction. The version of record of the high-mobility FIM–ISAC study states both halves of the trade-off explicitly: distributed Lorentz forces "enable rapid reconfiguration of the FIM surface shape within millisecond switching speeds", "comparable to typical channel coherence times in high-mobility wireless scenarios" [1, p. 13321]; and "the FIM surface shape can also be morphed once over several channel coherence intervals to achieve statistically optimal performance, thus offering a flexible trade-off between achievable performance gains and morphing speed requirements" [1, p. 13322]. These two halves pull in opposite directions, and both should be taken at face value. The second establishes that operating the geometry on a slower schedule than the fading is a design option the system literature already permits, so the conditional framing this review adopts in Section 5 is a premise supplied by that literature, not one imposed on it. The first is an assertion about another paper's hardware, and Section 5 traces it. A further FIM paper makes the fast reading more precise and equally untested: FIM surface shapes "are only updated on the timescale of the channel's coherence block" [32]. That is a legitimate modelling choice, and it asserts that command transport, actuation, settling and any recalibration all complete inside one coherence block.

Two costs are subtracted from whatever budget applies before any hardware acts. Pilot overhead scales with the controlled element count: the ON/OFF estimation protocol for a passive RIS requires 1 + M time slots to estimate the direct link and M reflected links sequentially [4, p. 720], while the FIM case acquires a two-dimensional measurement of Q subframes each containing T₂ time slots, with the element moving once per subframe and the phase adjusted once per time slot [3, p. 6829]. These are protocol units and we do not convert them to milliseconds, since the sources supply no numerology. The overhead nonetheless scales with the very quantity that makes a FIM attractive, and the FIM estimation protocol already contains a two-rate schedule. The hierarchical structure a system architect might propose as a solution is therefore present as a modelling premise, before any hardware has been asked whether it can meet either rate. Computation is likewise not free. One reviewed FIM paper reports wall-clock computation time, and it is the only such measurement on a FIM-specific algorithm in the reviewed set: a clustering mean-field variational sparse Bayesian learning estimator on a stated desktop processor rises from roughly 4 ms for a small virtual array to roughly 100 ms at a virtual array size of 324, with the slowest benchmark reaching about 1.2 s [3, Fig. 8, p. 6833].⁴ It bounds nothing for an embedded implementation, but it *is* a measurement, which distinguishes it from the iteration counts the other FIM papers report in place of durations, and it scales with virtual array size: the computation becomes more expensive as the movement becomes more ambitious.

---

⁴ Axis units read from the published figure, whose ordinate is labelled "Running time [Second]".

## 4. Hardware evidence across the adaptation chain

This section reports what has been measured. It is organised by *what was timed* rather than by tuning technology, because one of the review's findings — that electronic and mechanical ranges overlap — becomes invisible the moment the two are separated into different sections. Before any value can be compared with another, the type of quantity has to be named. Element switching, aperture configuration, mechanical element response, mechanical surface response, closed-loop convergence, open-loop actuation update rate and stabilised-radiation onset all recur here, and Supplementary Table S2 defines each with its start event, end event, timed object and the substitution it most often invites. Values may be compared only within a quantity type, and even then only when their objects and architectures match.

### 4.1 Flexible programmable reflective apertures

The flexible intelligent microwave metasurface with shape-guided adaptive programming [7] carries the most complete adaptation measurement in the reviewed set. The aperture is a 480 × 240 mm three-layer flexible sheet of metallic meta-atoms on polyimide, a polydimethylsiloxane substrate and a serpentine-mesh ground, with 32 × 16 meta-atoms at a 15 mm period and varactors driven over 0–30 V. Control granularity is columnar: the 32 columns share bias voltages, so the surface has 32 independently addressable channels, not 512 independent elements. Measured operation spans 3.0–3.4 GHz with up to approximately 270° of reflection-phase tuning across incidence angles from 0° to 45°, the normalised reflection amplitude staying above 0.4 across all bias and incidence combinations. We report that floor as the source reports it and do not convert it into a radiation or reflection efficiency, since the source does not define it as one and the conversion would need loss accounting the paper does not supply. Shape reconstruction from the 32 strain sensors is validated against a stereo reference at a root-mean-square deviation as low as 2.36 mm at a maximum displacement of 45 mm — an accuracy, not a timing.

Its timing decomposition is the only one of its kind in the reviewed set. Data preparation for the network inputs takes approximately 4 ms, about 2 ms of sensor reception at roughly 1200 Hz per channel plus about 2 ms of processing; inference across 32 channels takes approximately 2 ms; and the bias-voltage supply module responds in 5.25 ms. The components sum to 11.25 ms, a figure the paper's own timing figure annotates beside the measured total of 16.76 ms, the residual of approximately 5.5 ms arising from full-cycle control of all 32 channels over an RS-232 link at 115 200 bps [7, pp. 4–5; Supplementary Note 6]. Those components were not all timed the same way, which matters for how much weight each carries: the 4 ms and 2 ms figures are thread-timing averages taken inside the control program, while the 5.25 ms figure is an oscilloscope measurement of the supply module's output following a control signal. The supplement adds that deformation intervals must exceed 16.76 ms for voltage updates to remain synchronised, expressed as reliable operation at deformation frequencies up to 60 Hz, and projects without measuring that under 10 ms would be reachable with faster acquisition circuits and a different communication protocol.

The 16.76 ms figure requires three qualifications. It begins at shape *acquisition*, so it excludes the deformation that produced the shape. It ends at bias-voltage *supply*, so it excludes any mechanical settling and any interval before the far field is stable. And the deformation is externally imposed: the supplement describes the mechanical platform as a frame carrying two telescopic links and three movable fulcrums, adjusted by hand to set the curvature, with no actuation timing and no closed loop around the shape, so the system compensates for a shape it did not choose. The interval is therefore a compensation latency, and reading it as a FIM adaptation time would misattribute it by at least two stages at each end.

The same supplement reports a second, methodologically independent experiment which, uniquely in the reviewed set, terminates at electromagnetic output instead of a control signal. A finger-triggered sensor replaces the strain input; a dual-channel oscilloscope records the trigger on one channel and, on the other, received beam power demodulated by a logarithmic detector calibrated over −10 to −60 dBm at 3.1 GHz. The measured delay from trigger to stabilised RF output is 16.7 ms [7, Supplementary Note 6]. This review therefore does not claim that radio-frequency stabilisation is never timed in this literature. One condition travels with the figure: the geometry is static throughout, and the interval contains no shape change.

The platform also establishes a substantial application-level result. Mounted on an aerofoil model — the motivating scenario being aerofoil flutter under inertial, aerodynamic and elastic forces — it maintains a real-time QPSK video link at 3.1 GHz to a receiver 2 m away at 0° or 30°, with error vector magnitude staying around −20 dB while the surface is bent dynamically, and that demonstration is untimed. A second, independent flexible reconfigurable aperture confirms that such apertures are buildable: the conformal reconfigurable reflectarray of polydimethylsiloxane and printed liquid metal reaches 16.13 dBi peak gain with ±45° scanning at 9 GHz [21]. Its curvature is known a priori, it has no shape sensing, and it reports no timing of any kind.

### 4.2 Rigid electronically reconfigurable surfaces: the timing comparators

The scalable integrated RIS [5] is a one-bit PIN-diode surface at 9–10 GHz with 180° ± 20° phase difference, built as 16 × 16 tiles each carrying an Artix-7 FPGA, four tiles forming a 32 × 32 prototype. It reports an update time below 0.1 ms and a tile ON/OFF configuration update below 10 ms. Both are upper bounds, not measured means, and both concern the same object, contrary to how the pair is easily read. The abstract attaches the first to "each element", but no per-element measurement appears in the body: the figure traces to an end-to-end reconfiguration time for one 16 × 16 tile, about 40 μs over the Ethernet-based interfaces and up to 100 μs over USB/UART, against an internal FPGA update of about 40 ns once the configuration is stored [5, p. 6]. The second is the tile configuration update as operated in the near-field measurement campaign [5, pp. 8–9]. Both end at the configuration write, neither states an electromagnetic criterion, and as bounds they are mutually consistent. What separates them is the context in which each was stated, not the object or the technology. A reported latency without its start event, end event and object is not yet a comparable quantity. The same paper reports that the control network uses time-multiplexed latching, reducing the effective update rate to a quarter of the raw parallel speed, and reports what such a panel costs to run — 8.25 W with all diodes off, 13 W with all on, and 11.25–11.60 W during beam steering for the 32 × 32 array. Measured control power is rare in this literature and this is the only such figure in the reviewed set.

Those two bounds are *controller write* times in the sense of Supplementary Table S2: they run from a command issued by the compute element to the control state being written, and they say nothing about how long the tuning device itself takes to change state. The transition of the tuning material is a separate quantity type with its own start and end events, and the values reported for it in the reviewed set are numerically much larger without being measurements of the same thing. The liquid-crystal RIS based on defected delay lines [6] is the reviewed set's most carefully characterised material transition: a 4.6 μm liquid-crystal layer, 12 × 10 unit cells at 62 GHz, 6.8 GHz (10.9 %) bandwidth, insertion loss below 7 dB, and beam steering from −50° to +50°. Its measured response times are τ~on~ ≈ 15 ms and τ~off~ = 72 ms, strongly asymmetric. The 10 % and 90 % thresholds that delimit them are read from the markers on the source's response-time figure; the text defines τ~on~ and τ~off~ as the transitions between the two liquid-crystal permittivity states and states no threshold [6, Fig. 4a]. A projection of below 2 ms for a 1 μm layer appears in the same discussion and is explicitly not a measurement of the fabricated device. Read as material transitions alone, the values reported in the reviewed set run from approximately 15 ms, measured on the fabricated device, to the tens of seconds the same paper attributes to reflectarray-type liquid-crystal implementations [6, p. 7]; both endpoints are liquid crystal. The semiconductor end of that quantity type carries no figure at all, because no reviewed source measures a diode or varactor transition: the flexible metasurface calls its varactor switching negligibly short and reports no measurement of it [7], and the mechanism survey ranks modulation rates, not transition times [9]. Nothing here supports an inference that semiconductor transitions are slow, and nothing here places the sub-0.1 ms controller-write bound of [5] on the same scale as the 15 ms material transition of [6]. They are different quantity types, and on each technology only one of the two has been measured.

### 4.3 Commanded mechanical morphing, without a radio

The filamentary mechanical metasurface [22] achieves reversible out-of-plane deformation of about 30 % of an 18.0 mm sample using distributed Lorentz forces at currents below 27.5 mA in a 224 ± 16 mT field. Element response time is below 0.07 s, measured by monitoring a single serpentine beam with a 60 fps side camera and identifying the frame after which no displacement deviation is visible; system morphing is characterised as within 0.1 s. Its distinguishing feature is closed-loop control, with in-situ stereo imaging driving a gradient-based optimiser.

The cost of that loop is easy to miss, because it is fully visible only in the supplementary information. One function evaluation, comprising a voltage update, a wait for the sample to settle, a stereo capture with processing and a loss evaluation, costs 0.35 ± 0.15 s, of which 0.19 s is imaging and template matching and 0.1 s is a deliberate settling pause. Each optimiser iteration requires 4(N + M) + 2 function evaluations, which is 34 for a 4 × 4 sample, and convergence takes 5 to 15 iterations. The paper states the resulting figure directly: a 4 × 4 sample takes an average of approximately 2.5 minutes to morph into a shape from the zero-actuation initial state [22, Supplementary Note S6, Supplementary Table 1].

The separation between that figure and the platform's sub-0.1 s mechanics is large, and it is what the comparability classes exist to preserve: the element response cited downstream as evidence of feasibility (below 0.07 s) and the demonstrated closed-loop convergence (approximately 150 s) differ by a factor of roughly two thousand, and the reviewed system literature quotes neither. What takes 2.5 minutes is *searching* for the voltages that produce a target shape on a nonlinear structure with a camera in the loop. The same platform also runs open-loop at a 10 fps actuation update rate, and the two must not be joined: the sequences demonstrated at that rate are designed by the paper's model-driven inverse method, not replayed from voltages the closed-loop search found, and the source attaches the rate to those demonstrations specifically [22, Supplementary Videos 1–2]. Neither of the readings this invites is a law; both are properties of this platform. In the one demonstrated shape-control loop in the reviewed set, actuation is not the dominant contributor to loop time; sensing, perception and search are. Whether a radiating FIM would also be perception-limited depends on its sensing modality, its verification criterion and its compute load, none of which has been measured. Still, a closed-loop FIM's rate may be set by perception instead of actuation, which is a reason to instrument the sensing path early. No reviewed system model represents this stage at all. The same reported quantities also invite a substitution: multiplying the feedback-cycle time by the iteration count yields a convergence figure roughly two orders of magnitude below the value the source states directly, because an iteration here is 34 function evaluations instead of one cycle.

The soft shape-programmable surface [8] uses Lorentz-actuated liquid-metal microfluidic ribbons in an elastomer and reports a three-level decomposition that separates the quantities this review has to keep apart: an isolated ribbon responds in approximately 30 ms measured (approximately 50 ms by finite-element analysis); a full surface develops from flat in approximately 300 ms, of which approximately 250 ms is viscoelastic membrane relaxation; and shape-to-shape switching is stated as a sum rather than as a value: the time to develop the first shape (≈300 ms), the time to process the script for the next (≈50 ms), and the time to develop the second (≈300 ms). The ≈650 ms we quote is that sum, computed by us; the source prints no single figure for it. The element-to-surface penalty is a factor of ten, and the paper attributes it to the membrane, not the actuator, which matters because a membrane is a materials property. Both mechanical platforms show a penalty in the same direction but of very different size: a factor of about 1.4 for the filamentary mesh against about ten for the soft surface. The penalty therefore depends on construction, and no reviewed measurement establishes it for a radio-frequency stack.

### 4.4 Flexible active arrays: demonstrated capability, no reported duration

The flexible active antenna array work [23] demonstrates two 256-element, 30 × 30 cm arrays at mass densities around 0.1 g cm⁻² that remain fully functional and programmable at concave and convex bend radii below 23 cm, and deliver approximately 80 mW of DC power wirelessly to a receiver about a metre away. The demonstrated steering and focusing ranges are stated by the authors to be limited by the measurement range, not by the array. This is the closest any reviewed source comes to the operation a FIM would need after changing shape — re-establishing coherent aperture behaviour on a deformed, large, real radiating surface under closed-loop feedback — and it reports no duration for that operation. One qualification applies: this is an active transmitter with per-element RFICs, phase-locked loops and on-chip self-sensing receivers, not a passive reflector, and its calibration strategy depends on exactly that.

The values in Table 2 measure different processes on different objects with different start events, and cannot be pooled. They support ordinal comparison within a quantity type, and Figure 2 displays them accordingly.

> **Figure 2.** *The timing landscape of the reviewed evidence.* Lanes are separate because the quantities are not commensurable: each was measured on a different object and architecture, between a different pair of start and end events. The axis shows where the reported values fall; it is not a latency budget, and no value may be pooled with, ranked against or substituted for a value in another lane. Two lanes carry no value at all — the mechanics of a radiating aperture, and its settling after a commanded morph. The two mechanical-loop lanes belong to the *same* platform and differ by more than three orders of magnitude, because one actuates from voltages the platform's model supplies and the other searches for voltages it does not have. *(File: `figures/fig2_timing_landscape.pdf`.)*

Displayed on that axis, the reported ranges qualify the standard dichotomy. Mechanical movement is generally slower than electronic reconfiguration, as the closest survey states qualitatively [11], and that is a reasonable first approximation which cannot be applied from an architecture label alone. An electronic material transition on one platform (72 ms) is numerically larger than a measured partial electronic chain on another (16.76 ms) and lies within a factor of about four of a full mechanical surface morph on a third (≈300 ms). Those three values were obtained at different frequencies, on different mechanisms, on different objects, with different start and end events, and they sit in three different quantity types. They may be displayed on a common axis to show that their reported ranges overlap. They must not be treated as like-for-like performance measurements, pooled statistically, or used to infer the bottleneck of an integrated architecture. Architecture labels alone therefore do not establish a universal latency ordering. "Fast electronics, slow mechanics" holds only with mechanism-, object- and architecture-specific qualification, and which stage binds must be established for the specific combination of material, actuator, control network and aperture in question.

### 4.6 Coverage of the chain, and where it stops

The per-source coding in Supplementary Section S6 yields three counts, and they are not interchangeable, so each is stated with the axis it counts. Quantitatively evidenced stages: the maximum is six, reached by [7] and [22]. Measured stage durations: the maximum is four, reached by [22] alone. Stages carrying any duration information, whether measured or apportioned out of an aggregate: the maximum is six, reached by [7].

The platform that measures four stage durations is the filamentary mechanical metasurface [22], which times sensing, geometry estimation, control transmission and morphing, each with its own value and dispersion in its supplementary budget, and which has no radio-frequency layer at all. The flexible microwave metasurface [7] measures three — inference, electronic update, and stabilised radiation in the separate static-geometry experiment — and apportions three more out of its measured compensation-loop total, of which the control-transmission figure is a residual rather than a measurement. It does not command its geometry. Counted on the axis that permits comparison, the two sets overlap at sensing, geometry estimation, optimisation and control transmission, and differ exactly where the question lies: [7] carries the radio-frequency stages and cannot command a shape, while [22] carries the mechanical stages and does not radiate. Neither can be extended into the other by further measurement. Every other source is sparser still: one measured stage duration each for the liquid-crystal panel [6] and the soft shape-programmable surface [8]; none for the scalable integrated RIS [5], whose two reported bounds end at a configuration write rather than at a meta-atom state change, and therefore bound an aggregate containing that stage instead of timing it; and none for the flexible active array [23], which demonstrates seven of the ten stages as working operations and attaches a duration to none of them.

Figure 3 shows the pattern by architecture class. Read across it, the stages sit on mutually incompatible platforms: measured morphing durations exist only on A4 platforms with no radio-frequency layer; no platform in the reviewed set measures a settling duration at all, the closest figures being a component identified within an aggregate on one A4 platform and a deliberately allocated wait on the other; and electronic state transitions are timed only on A5 rigid panels and one A3 flexible aperture. Sensing, inference and control transport on a flexible radiating surface are timed only on an A3 platform where geometry is a disturbance rather than a control variable, and post-deformation calibration on a deformable radiating aperture is demonstrated only on an A7 active transmitter, without a duration there or anywhere else in the reviewed set. Stabilised radiation is the clearest case for keeping the two axes apart: five platforms establish it quantitatively through patterns, gain, scan range, insertion loss or delivered power [5, 6, 7, 21, 23], and the one that attaches a duration to it holds its geometry static [7]. The gap is therefore not that stabilised radiation is unevidenced; it is that its onset after a commanded shape change goes unmeasured.

> **Figure 3.** *Adaptation-chain coverage by architecture class.* Rows are platform classes rather than individual papers; each cell records the strongest evidence any platform in that class provides for that stage. Fill colour gives the stage evidence status, and the appended marker gives the separate question of what is known about duration: **·T** a measured stage duration, **·(T)** a duration available only as a share, component or residual of an aggregate, **·[R]** a rate rather than a duration, and no marker untimed. The one cell that would carry an allocated interval — mechanical settling on the commanded-mechanical class — is marked † and carries no measured duration in either case. Several cells are quantitatively measured and carry no timing marker, because a radiation pattern, a gain figure or a delivered power is a measurement but not a timing. *(File: `figures/fig3_adaptation_chain.pdf`.)*

A total could in principle be assembled by taking each stage from wherever it was measured: the electronic loop from A3, plus surface morphing from A4, plus unmeasured settling and calibration terms. Such a sum would concatenate measurements taken on four different physical objects, one of which has no meta-atoms, another of which cannot bend, and none of which has both a controlled geometry and a measured radiation pattern. It would have the appearance of an engineering estimate while adding quantities that are not commensurable. The decomposition licenses something weaker and more defensible: within the reviewed set, no source times the adaptation chain end to end on any single object, and the reason is architectural, not incidental.

Six capabilities nonetheless reach prototype-measurement level or higher: large flexible apertures that still radiate; in-situ shape sensing on three platforms; electronic phase reconfiguration timed at the controller; deformation-aware electronic compensation demonstrated over the air; commanded mechanical shape control with closed-loop verification; and conformal design at fixed curvature. None of these constituent capabilities is absent from the reviewed evidence base when considered separately, and separate demonstrations of them do not establish that they cease to constrain the design once combined, since integration changes the mass, the damping, the control granularity and the calibration burden of each. No reviewed source measures the intersection, and Section 5 states that as the validation gap.

---

## 5. High-mobility feasibility and the validation gap

### 5.1 A stage-resolved answer

Assembling the demand side of Section 3 with the evidence of Section 4, the review question admits a stage-resolved answer instead of a verdict. Table 3 gives it, under one convention that matters. The "must it track fast fading?" column records a consequence of a stated assumption, not a finding, and the assumption is named in the cell. The central question of this review is which stages are exempt, and a table that presupposed its own answer would not be informative.
